options.content: The accuracy, completeness and consistency of data
options.rationale: Correct: integrity means the data can be trusted to be correct.

options.content: Keeping data hidden from people who are not allowed to see it
options.rationale: That is privacy (confidentiality).

options.content: Making a second copy of data in case it is lost
options.rationale: That is a backup, one way of protecting integrity.

options.content: Scrambling data so that it cannot be read when intercepted
options.rationale: That is encryption, a privacy measure.

explanation: Data integrity is about data being accurate, complete and consistent throughout its life.

options.content: A learner's name and home address
options.rationale: Correct: it identifies a living person.

options.content: The average mark of a whole province
options.rationale: An average does not identify any individual.

options.content: The number of computers in a school lab
options.rationale: This is not about a person.

options.content: The opening hours of a clinic in Bulawayo
options.rationale: This is information about an organisation.

explanation: Personal data is any information that relates to an identifiable living person.

stem: A hospital receptionist can view appointment times but **not** test results. Which measure is being used?

options.content: Data validation
options.rationale: Validation checks input is sensible; it does not limit who can see data.

options.content: Data backup
options.rationale: Backups protect against loss, not unauthorised viewing.

options.content: Access levels
options.rationale: Correct: each user account is given only the permissions its job needs.

options.content: Data verification
options.rationale: Verification checks data was entered or copied accurately.

explanation: Access levels (access rights) control which data each user may see and whether they can change it.

stem: Under data protection principles, a shop that collects customers' phone numbers to send delivery messages should **not**:

options.content: Keep the numbers secure with passwords
options.rationale: Keeping data secure is required, not forbidden.

options.content: Correct a number when a customer reports a mistake
options.rationale: Keeping data accurate is required.

options.content: Delete the numbers when they are no longer needed
options.rationale: Not keeping data longer than necessary is a principle.

options.content: Sell the numbers to another company for advertising
options.rationale: Correct: data must be used only for the purpose for which it was collected.

explanation: Personal data may be used only for the stated purpose. Selling it for advertising without consent breaks that principle.

stem: A school's laptop holding learners' records might be stolen. Which measure would **best** keep the records private if this happens?

options.content: Running a daily backup of the records
options.rationale: A backup restores the data but does not stop the thief reading it.

options.content: Adding a range check to the marks field
options.rationale: Validation improves accuracy, not privacy.

options.content: Encrypting the hard disk
options.rationale: Correct: without the key the thief cannot read the data.

options.content: Using double entry when typing the records
options.rationale: Verification improves accuracy, not privacy.

explanation: Encryption scrambles the data, so a stolen disk cannot be understood without the decryption key.
hints: Which measure makes a stolen file unreadable?

stem: A power cut during saving corrupts a shop's stock file, so several quantities become wrong. What has been affected?

options.content: Data privacy
options.rationale: No one has seen data they should not.

options.content: Data integrity
options.rationale: Correct: the data is no longer accurate.

options.content: Software copyright
options.rationale: Copyright is not involved.

options.content: User consent
options.rationale: Consent concerns permission to collect data.

explanation: Corrupted, inaccurate data is a loss of integrity. Privacy is not involved because nobody has gained unauthorised access.
hints: Has anyone seen data they should not, or is the data wrong?

stem: A bank wants to find out which member of staff changed a customer's address last week. What should its system keep?

options.content: A firewall log of blocked websites
options.rationale: This records network traffic, not data changes.

options.content: A presence check on the address field
options.rationale: Validation does not record who made changes.

options.content: An audit trail
options.rationale: Correct: it logs who changed which data and when.

options.content: A copy of the privacy policy
options.rationale: A policy states rules but records nothing.

explanation: An audit trail records each change with the user ID and time, so changes can be traced and integrity checked.
hints: Which measure records who changed what?

stem: Marks in a college database have been altered dishonestly by someone using a shared staff login. Which change would **most** improve integrity?

options.content: Ask all lecturers to change the shared password every year
options.rationale: A shared login still hides who made each change.

options.content: Add validation so that every mark must be between 0 and 100
options.rationale: Dishonest marks within range still pass validation.

options.content: Back up the whole database to a cloud service at the end of every term
options.rationale: Backups help recovery but do not stop or trace changes.

options.content: Give each lecturer a unique login with edit rights for their own classes only
options.rationale: Correct: changes are limited and every change can be traced to one person.

explanation: Unique accounts with limited access rights stop unauthorised edits and make every change traceable to a person.
hints: Which option addresses unauthorised changes AND tracing them?

stem: Data can be kept completely private and still be inaccurate.
explanation: True. Privacy and integrity are different: a record can be well protected from unauthorised people and still contain a typing error.

stem: In Zimbabwe, personal data protection is set out in the Cyber and Data Protection Act.
explanation: True. The Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] (2021) sets out data protection principles in Zimbabwe.

stem: Match each measure to what it does.

right.content: Records who changed data and when
Keeps a copy so lost data can be restored
Makes data unreadable without a key
Limit which data each user may see or change

explanation: Encryption: unreadable without the key. Access levels: limit users. Audit trail: records changes. Backup: allows recovery.

stem: Classify each incident as mainly a breach of privacy or a loss of integrity.

left.content: A clerk tells a friend a customer's account balance
A learner's mark is typed as 18 instead of 81
A phone company's customer list is posted online
Two copies of a patient's record show different blood groups

explanation: Disclosure to unauthorised people breaks privacy; wrong or inconsistent data is a loss of integrity.
hints: Privacy: someone sees data they should not. Integrity: data becomes wrong.

payload.template: Personal data must be adequate, relevant and not {{blank:a}}. It must not be kept for {{blank:b}} than necessary. It must be collected with the person's {{blank:c}} or another lawful reason.

explanation: Not excessive; not kept longer than necessary; collected with consent.
hints: One principle concerns how much data, another how long.

stem: Name the Zimbabwean regulator given the role of data protection authority under the Cyber and Data Protection Act (its abbreviation is enough).

accepted.value: Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe

explanation: POTRAZ, the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe, acts as the data protection authority.

stem: Explain the difference between data privacy and data integrity.

points.description: Privacy: personal data is kept away from unauthorised people / individuals control how it is used
Integrity: data is accurate, complete and consistent (can be trusted)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Privacy means only authorised people can see or use someone's personal data. Integrity means the data is accurate, complete and consistent, so it can be trusted.

explanation: Privacy is about who may see and use data; integrity is about whether the data is correct.
hints: Who sees it versus is it correct.

stem: A pharmacy in Masvingo keeps customers' prescriptions on a computer. Suggest **two** measures to protect the privacy of the data and **two** measures to protect its integrity.

points.description: Privacy: unique user IDs and strong passwords / access levels so only pharmacists see prescriptions
Privacy: encryption / firewall / screens that lock automatically / staff confidentiality training
Integrity: validation of input (e.g. range check on dose) / verification (double entry or visual check)
Integrity: regular backups / audit trail of changes / restricted edit rights

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Give each pharmacist a unique login with access levels so cashiers cannot view prescriptions, and encrypt the database. Use a range check on doses with a visual check of each prescription, and back the data up every day.

explanation: Privacy measures restrict who sees data; integrity measures keep the data correct and recoverable.
hints: Two measures for privacy, two for integrity.

stem: Bulawayo Community Clinic (fictional) stores patient records on a network. Receptionists book appointments; nurses record test results; doctors write diagnoses.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which access level should a receptionist have for patients' test results?

options.content: Read only
options.rationale: Even reading is more than the job needs.

options.content: No access
options.rationale: Correct: booking appointments does not need test results.

options.content: Read and edit
options.rationale: Receptionists do not record results.

options.content: Full control, including delete
options.rationale: This would risk privacy and integrity.

parts.explanation: Users get only the access their job needs.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Classify each incident at the clinic.

left.content: A nurse reads a famous patient's record out of curiosity
A test result is saved under the wrong patient

parts.explanation: Unauthorised viewing: privacy. Wrong data: integrity.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe **three** data protection principles the clinic must follow.

points.description: A principle stated clearly (e.g. collected fairly and lawfully with consent)
A second principle (e.g. used only for the stated purpose / not excessive)
A third principle (e.g. kept accurate and up to date / kept secure / not kept longer than necessary / patients may see their data)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The clinic must collect only the data it needs to treat patients, use it only for treatment and not share it with advertisers, and keep it secure with passwords and access levels.

explanation: (a) No access. (b) Curiosity reading: privacy; wrong patient: integrity.
hints: Each user should only see what their job needs.
Is the problem who saw it, or whether it is correct?

stem: At Chipo's school, all teachers use one shared login, *staff1*, to enter marks into the database. A learner's mark was found to have been changed from 45 to 85.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: A range check of 0 to 100 on the marks field would have rejected the changed mark.
parts.explanation: False: 85 is within the range 0 to 100, so it passes validation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the shared login makes it hard to protect the integrity of the marks.

points.description: It is impossible to trace which teacher made the change (no accountability)
Anyone who knows the password can change any mark / cannot restrict teachers to their own classes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Because everyone uses staff1, the school cannot tell who changed the mark, and every teacher can edit every class's marks instead of only their own.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Recommend **two** improvements and explain how each helps.

points.description: Unique user IDs and passwords for each teacher, so changes can be traced
Access levels limiting edits to own classes / an audit trail logging changes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Give each teacher their own login and password so every change can be traced, and keep an audit trail that records each change to a mark with the user and time.

hints: A shared login hides who did what.
Validation only checks data is sensible.
